title: The American Scholar
hookLine: a talk urging people to think for themselves, not only from books
last: THE WORLD WEARS THE COLORS OF MY SPIRIT.

cards: A hall full of educated men, gathered for a college society's yearly speech. They expect something polished about learning and books. Emerson stands up and, politely, tells them books can be a danger.

Not that books are bad. That a person can read so much of other people's thinking that they forget to do any of their own. He has a name for what he wants instead, two words he keeps coming back to: Man Thinking.
Not a thinker as a job title. A person, actually thinking.

teach.b: First, what the scholar is. In the right state, Emerson says, the scholar is Man Thinking. In the wrong state, a mere thinker, or worse, "the parrot of other men's thinking."
A parrot can repeat anything; it just can't mean it. Second, what books are for. "Books are the best of things, well used; abused, among the worst."

teach.h: BOOKS ARE FOR NOTHING BUT TO INSPIRE.
teach.b: And more sharply: "They are for nothing but to inspire." A book isn't meant to do your thinking. It's meant to light the fire under your own.
Third, the warning, and it has humor in it.

Emerson describes meek young men growing up in libraries, believing it's their duty to accept the views of the great authors, and forgetting that those authors were once only young men in libraries too, when they wrote their books.
Fourth, where else the scholar learns. Books are one teacher in this talk.
Emerson also names nature, the world around you, and action, actually living and working. Thinking for yourself doesn't mean ignoring what came before.
It means letting what you read, see and do all feed a mind that's awake. Away from lecture halls, this is small. You read a headline and notice you've already borrowed someone's opinion of it.
You hear a strong view at work and nod before you've checked whether you agree. Emerson's question isn't whether the view is right. It's whether it's yours.

how: Readers of The American Scholar often take its call to be 'Man Thinking' as a reminder to treat books as a spark for their own thinking rather than a substitute for it.

games.why: "they are for nothing but to inspire." read them, and then think.

practice: Pick a question you have an opinion on, something you've mostly heard other people answer, and for now set those voices aside.

Ask what you've actually seen and what you know from your own life, and follow your own thought one slow step at a time. You may end up exactly where you started, and that's fine: this time, you walked there.
